title: The many ways to reorder
question: How do we describe and count the ways to rearrange a set of things?
hook: Anagrams, shuffled lists and codebreaking all rest on one idea of rearranging.
idea: A permutation rearranges a set, and n distinct objects can be ordered in n factorial ways.

beats.prompt: You apply shuffle A to a deck and then shuffle B. A friend applies B first and then A. Do you end up with the same order?

choices.label: Always the same
choices.feedback: Tempting because both use the same two shuffles, but order of application matters in general.

choices.label: Same unless the deck is large
choices.feedback: Deck size is not what decides it; composition is not commutative in general.

beats.explain: Composition of two permutations is in general not commutative, so applying them in opposite orders typically gives different results.

beats.prompt: match each term to its meaning
pairs: A permutation with no fixed points
Exchanges two elements, leaves the rest fixed
An ordered sequence of k distinct elements
beats.explain: Each term describes a different feature of a rearrangement: single elements, the whole shuffle, a two-element swap, or an ordered selection.

beats.prompt: put these events in order, earliest first
items: Xenocrates counts possible Greek syllables (396-314 BC)
Al-Khalil lists Arabic words with permutations and combinations (717-786)
Lagrange studies permutations of polynomial roots (around 1770)
Rejewski uses cycle types against Enigma (1932-1933)
beats.explain: The dates run from the 4th century BC through the 8th century and the 1770s to the 1930s.

beats.prompt: one step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: Start with three cards in positions 1, 2 and 3.
Swap the first two cards and leave the third card where it is.
Card 3 stays in its position, so the shuffle has a fixed point.
A shuffle with a fixed point is a derangement.
beats.explain: A derangement is a permutation with no fixed points, so a shuffle that leaves card 3 in place is not one.
